readings.c1s3: Impulse-wheel''', a form of turbine water-wheel driven by the impulse of a jet.—'''Intermittent, internal, lapidary wheel.''' See the adjectives.—'''Large wheel.''' See ''spinning-wheel.''—'''Long wheel''', a workmen’s name for a grindstone driven by a belt and a hand-wheel 5 or 6 feet in diameter, which is turned by a laborer stationed behind the grinder.—'''Mansell wheel''', a railroad-wheel in which the hub is composed of two wrought- or cast-iron rings bolted together. ''Car-Builder’s Dict.''—'''Middle-shot wheel''', in ''hydraul.'', a breast-wheel which receives the water at about the middle of its height. See cut under ''breast-wheel.''—'''Multiple wheel''', a form of slosh-wheel.—'''Multiplying wheel''', a form of multiplying gearing; a geared wheel for converting slower movement into more rapid movement. Compare cut under ''lantern-wheel.''—'''Mutilated wheel.''' See ''mutilated'' (with cut).—'''Non-circular wheel''', a wheel having a perimeter which is not circular, but is elliptical, scroll-shaped, hyperbolar, etc. Two such wheels are employed for transmitting a velocity of variable ratio between a pair of parallel axes. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''Persian wheel''', a water-lifting wheel; a bucket-wheel or noria; an apparatus in which buckets, jars, or box-chambers are arranged in a radial position on a large wheel, which by its revolution dips the vessels in the water, fills them, and raises each in turn to empty its load on another level. It is used especially for irrigation. Compare cut under ''noria.''—'''Pitch-back wheel''', a form of water-wheel in which the water, before descending into the buckets, is turned at an angle with its course in the flume: a kind of breast-wheel in which the water-supply is near the top of the wheel.—'''Potters’ wheel.''' See ''potter''<sup>1</sup> (with cut).—'''Savart’s wheel''', an acoustical instrument, consisting of a toothed wheel which can be rapidly rotated so as to strike against a card and produce a tone, the vibration-number of which can be accurately determined from the number of the revolutions of the wheel. Compare ''siren'' (with cut).—'''Saxon wheel.''' See ''spinning-wheel.''—'''Skew
readings.c2s1:
—'''Spiral wheels''', in ''mach.'', a form of gearing in which the teeth are formed upon the circumference of cylinders of the required diameter at an angle with their respective axes. By this construction the teeth become in fact small parts of screws or spirals winding round the cylinders (whence the name). Wheels of this kind are often used when the two shafts require to pass each other. When the shafts are in the same plane bevel-wheels are employed.—'''Split wheel.''' See ''split gear'', under ''split''.—'''Sun-and-planet wheels.''' See ''sun''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To break a butterfly (fly''', etc.''') upon a (the) wheel''', to subject one to a punishment out of all proportion to the gravity of the offense and the importance of the offender; hence, to employ great means or exertions for the attainment of trifling ends.
{{smaller block|<poem>Satire or sense, alas! can Sporus feel,
Who ''breaks a butterfly upon a wheel?''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 308.}}
He was sorry . . . for the excellent people, and deplored the necessity of ''breaking'' mere ''house-flies on the wheel.''
{{right|''Dickens'', Little Dorrit, ii. 21.}}}}
'''To break upon the wheel.''' See ''break''.—'''Toothed wheels.''' See ''toothed''.—'''To put a spoke in one’s wheel.''' See ''spoke''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To put one’s shoulder to the wheel.''' See ''shoulder''.—'''To slack over the wheel.''' See ''slack''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To steer a trick at the wheel.''' See ''steer''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Undershot wheel.''' See ''undershot''.—'''Variable-speed wheels.''' See ''variable''.—'''Waved wheel''', in ''mech.'', a friction-wheel having a waved or convoluted surface, and imparting a reciprocating motion to an arc or lever pressing against its side. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''Wheel and axle''', one of the mechanical powers, consisting in its primary form of a cylindrical axle on which a wheel, concentric with the axle, is firmly fastened. A rope is usually attached to the wheel; the axle is turned by means of a lever; and the rope acts as in the pulley—that is, also upon the principle of the lever.—'''Wheel barometer''', a modification of the siphon barometer. See ''barometer''.—'''Wheel couching.''' See ''couching''<sup>1</sup>, 5.—'''Wheel crossbow''', a crossbow in which the bow is bent by the revolutions of a wheel acting as a windlass. See cut under ''moulinet''.—'''Wheel-cutting machine.''' (''a'') A gear-cutting machine. (''b'') A device for dividing a circle

'''8.''' To shape by means of the wheel, as in pottery. See ''potters’ wheel'' (under ''potter''<sup>1</sup>), and ''throw''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', 2.—'''9.''' To break upon the wheel. See ''break''.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To turn on or as on an axis or about a center; rotate; revolve.
{{smaller block|<poem>His Glory found
  Thou first Mobile,
  Which mak’st all ''wheel''
In circle round.</poem>
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|The moon . . . not once ''wheeling'' upon her own center.
{{right|''Bentley.''}}}}
'''2.''' To change direction of course, as if moving on a pivot or center.
{{smaller block|<poem>As he to flight his ''wheeling'' car addrest,
The speedy jav’lin drove from back to breast.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, v. 53.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Steady! steady! the masses of men
''Wheel'', and fall in, and ''wheel'' again,
Softly as circles drawn with pen.</poem>
{{right|''Leigh Hunt'', Captain Sword and Captain Pen, ii.}}}}
'''3.''' To move in a circular or spiral course.
{{smaller block|Then ''wheeling'' down the steep of heaven he flies.
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The poor gold fish eternally ''wheeling'' round his crystal wall.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The swallow ''wheeled'' above high up in air.
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 15.}}}}
'''4.''' To take a circular course; return upon one’s steps; hence, to wander; go out of the straight
readings.c3s2:
way.
{{smaller block|<poem>Spies of the Volsces
Held me in chase, that I was forced to ''wheel''
Three or four miles about, else had I, sir,
Half an hour since brought my report.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 6. 19.}}}}

'''5.''' To travel smoothly; go at a round pace; trundle along; roll forward.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thunder mix’d with hail,
Hail mix’d with fire, must rend the Egyptian sky
And ''wheel'' on the earth, devouring where it rolls.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 183.}}
<poem>Through the rough copse ''wheel'' thou with hasty stride;
I choose to saunter o’er the grassy plain.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', River Duddon, xxx.}}}}

'''6.''' To move on wheels; specifically, to ride a bicycle or tricycle; travel by means of a bicycle or tricycle. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|The sun, gladdened by the sweet air, shone on the fields and woods, and the ugly barracks and pretty cottages by which we ''wheeled.''
{{right|''J. and E. R. Pennell'', Canterbury Pilgrimage on a [Tricycle.}}}}

'''7.''' To change or reverse one’s opinion or course of action: frequently with ''about.''
{{smaller block|Being able to advance no further, they are in a fair way to ''wheel about'' to the other extreme. {{right|''South.''}}
<poem>Plato and Aristotle were at a losse,
And ''wheel’d about'' again to spell Christ-Crosse.</poem>
{{right|''G. Herbert'', The Temple, The Church Militant.}}}}

'''wheel<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''wheal''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wheel<sup>3</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''wheal''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wheel<sup>4</sup>''' (hwēl), ''n.'' An erroneous dialectal form of ''weel''<sup>2</sup>.

'''3.''' A circular course or motion; a whirling round; a revolution; rotation; also, a wheeling, turning, or bending.
{{smaller block|<poem>The leed, withouten faile,
Is, lo, the metal of Saturne,
That hath a ful large ''wheel'' to turne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1450.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Satan, bowing low, . . .
Throws his steep flight in many an aery ''wheel''.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 741.}}}}
'''4.''' A motive power; in the plural, machinery; hence, a principle of life or motion.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''wheels'' of weary life at last stood still.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden and Lee'', Œdipus, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That power who bids the ocean ebb and flow, . . .
Builds life on death, on change duration founds,
And gives the eternal ''wheels'' to know their rounds.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 168.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When . . . the heart is sick,
And all the ''wheels'' of Being slow.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, l.}}}}
'''5†.''' The burden of a song; a refrain: perhaps in allusion to its regular recurrence.   ''Steevens.''
{{smaller block|<poem>''Oph.'' [Sings.] You must sing a-down a-down,</poem> An you call him a-down-a.
O, how the ''wheel'' becomes it!
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 5. 172.}}}}
'''6.''' A factory for grinding cutlery. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|This branch of trade [cutlery grinding] is, in Sheffield, conducted in distinct establishments called ''wheels''.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VI. 734.}}}}
'''7.''' A dollar.   ''Tufts.'' [Thieves’ jargon.]—'''8.''' In ''embroidery'' and ''fancy needlework'', an opening, not necessarily circular, filled with radiating bars or brides of thread. {{smaller|It is a common form of decoration for collars and similar washable garments. Sometimes the radiating lines are interspersed with loops, festoons, and the like, or are of different lengths, so that a part of the opening will be filled with more bands than another part, producing diversity of pattern.}}
'''9.''' See ''ward''<sup>2</sup>, 11.—'''Adhesion of wheels to rails.''' {{smaller|See ''adhesion''.}}—'''Aërohydrodynamic wheel.''' {{smaller|See ''aërohydrodynamic''.}}—'''Bastard wheel.''' {{smaller|See ''bastard''.}}—'''Big wheel.''' {{smaller|Same as ''large wheel''. It enables any person to confide an infant to the care of the asylum without being seen.}}
{{smaller block|The ruota or ''foundling-wheel'' still exists in 1222 of the communes, being frequent in the Neapolitan provinces and Sicily.

'''wheel<sup>1</sup>''' (hwēl), ''v.''   [< ME. *''whelen, whielen, hweolen''; < ''wheel''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to turn, or to move in a circle; make to rotate, revolve, or change direction.
{{smaller block|<poem>So had he seen, in fair Castile,
The youth in glittering squadrons start;
Suddenly the flying jennet ''wheel'',
And hurl the unexpected dart.</poem>
{{right|''Scott,'' L. of L. M., ii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|The sun gradually ''wheeled'' his broad disk down into the west.
{{right|''Irving,'' Sketch-Book, p. 438.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Sun flies forward to his brother Sun;
The dark Earth follows ''wheel’d'' in her ellipse;
And human things returning on themselves
Move onward, leading up the golden year.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Golden Year.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To ''wheel'' the wild scrub cattle at the yard
With a running fire of stockwhips and a fiery run of hoofs.</poem>
{{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', LII. 405.}}}}
'''2.''' To convey on wheels or in a vehicle mounted on wheels.
{{smaller block|You shall clap her into a post-chaise, . . . ''wheel'' her down to Scotland. {{right|''Colman'', Jealous Wife, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|“''Wheel'' me a little farther,” said her ladyship. “They will follow.” I obeyed her again, and ''wheeled'' her away from the house with extreme slowness.
{{right|''D. Christie Murray'', Weaker Vessel, xxxviii.}}}}
'''3.''' To make or perform in a circle; give a circular direction or form to.
{{smaller block|<poem>Now heaven in all her glory shone, and roll’d
Her motions, as the great first Mover’s hand
First ''wheel’d'' their course. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 501.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The silvered kite
In many a whistling circle ''wheels'' her flight.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', An Evening Walk.}}}}
'''4.''' To provide with a wheel or wheels: as, to ''wheel'' a cart.   ''Imp. Dict.''—'''5.''' To cause to move on or as on wheels; rotate; cause to turn: as, to ''wheel'' a rank of soldiers.
{{smaller block|Let fall the curtains, ''wheel'' the sofa round.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 37.}}}}
'''6†.''' To turn on a wheel.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fortune on lofte
And under eft gan hem to ''whielen'' bothe.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 139.}}}} wheel. See ''pinwheel'', 2.
{{smaller block|The skins next go into the England wheel vat . . . and are ''wheeled.''
{{right|''C. T. Davis'', Leather, p. 530.}}}}
'''8.''' To shape by means of the wheel, as in pottery. See ''potters’ wheel'' (under ''potter''<sup>1</sup>), and ''throw''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', 2.—'''9.''' To break upon the wheel. See ''break''.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To turn on or as on an axis or about a center; rotate; revolve.
{{smaller block|<poem>His Glory found

In circle round.</poem>
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|The moon . . . not once ''wheeling'' upon her own center.

'''2.''' To change direction of course, as if moving on a pivot or center.
{{smaller block|<poem>As he to flight his ''wheeling'' car addrest,

{{smaller block|Then ''wheeling'' down the steep of heaven he flies.

'''5.''' To travel smoothly; go at a round pace; trundle along; roll forward.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thunder mix’d with hail,

'''6.''' To move on wheels; specifically, to ride a bicycle or tricycle; travel by means of a bicycle or tricycle. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|The sun, gladdened by the sweet air, shone on the fields and woods, and the ugly barracks and pretty cottages by which we ''wheeled.''
{{right|''J. and E. R. Pennell'', Canterbury Pilgrimage on a [Tricycle.}}}}

{{smaller block|Being able to advance no further, they are in a fair way to ''wheel about'' to the other extreme. {{right|''South.''}}}}

'''wheel<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''wheal''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wheel<sup>3</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''wheal''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wheel<sup>4</sup>''' (hwēl), ''n.'' An erroneous dialectal form of ''weel''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wheelage''' (hwē′lạ̄j), ''n.''   [< ''wheel''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age''.]   A duty or toll paid for carts, etc., passing over certain ground.

'''wheel-animal''' (hwēl′an″i-ma̤l), ''n.'' A wheel-animalcule.

'''wheel-animalcule''' (hwēl′an-i-mal″kūl), ''n.'' A rotifer. See ''Rotifera'' (with cut), also cuts under ''Floscularia'', ''Rotifer'', and ''trochal''.

'''wheel-band''' (hwēl′band), ''n.'' The tire of a wheel.
{{smaller block|<poem>The chariot tree was drown’d in blood, and th’ arches by the seat
Dispurpled from the horses’ hoofs, and from the ''wheel-bands’'' beat.</poem>{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xi. 466.}}}}

'''wheel-barometer''' (hwēl′bạ-rom″e-tėr), ''n.'' See ''barometer''.

'''wheelbarrow''' (hwēl′bar″ō), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whelbarowe''; < ''wheel''<sup>1</sup> + ''barrow''<sup>2</sup>.]   A barrow with one wheel or more, on which it runs. {{smaller|The most common form has one wheel in front and two legs at the rear on which it rests, and two handles by which a person lifts the legs from the ground and carries a part of the load, while he pushes forward the vehicle on the wheel. Express and railroad barrows have two and often three or four wheels, only a small part of the load or none of it being carried by the person using the barrow, or truck, as it is more commonly called. Barrows of this class are commonly made with the wheels toward the middle and handles at each end for convenience in using on narrow steamboat-landings and station-platforms.}}
{{smaller block|Carrióla, . . . a ''wheel-barrow''. {{right|''Florio.''}}}}
{{smaller block|My author saith he saw some sixteen or twenty carpenters at work upon an engine, or carriage, for six muskets, manageable by one man, and to be crowded before him like a ''wheelbarrow'' upon wheels.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', II. 87.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
